items.title: Sprinting and marathon running use chemically different fuels
items.claim: Aerobic respiration of one glucose produces about 30-32 ATP. Anaerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP. Yet sprinters rely on the anaerobic path. Why use a pathway that wastes 94% of glucose's chemical energy?

options.text: It's faster — sprint muscle can produce ATP via glycolysis ~100x faster per second than oxidative phosphorylation can. Power output wins over efficiency in short bursts

items.reveal:
Aerobic respiration is the efficient long path: glycolysis (cytoplasm) -> pyruvate -> Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) -> oxidative phosphorylation -> ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with CO2 and water as byproducts.

Anaerobic glycolysis stops at pyruvate, converts it to lactate (regenerating the NAD+ glycolysis needs), and quits. Yield: 2 ATP per glucose. But it runs without oxygen and at ~100x the rate of mitochondrial ATP synthesis.

Sprint events (100m, weightlifting): mostly anaerobic. Lactate builds up. Burns. The 'oxygen debt' you owe after sprinting is the cost of clearing the lactate and replenishing phosphocreatine.

Endurance events (marathon, cycling): mostly aerobic, fuelled by glucose at first, then fat. Fat yields ~106 ATP per palmitate molecule but is metabolised slowly — fine for steady output.

Yeasts do alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate -> ethanol + CO2) instead of lactate fermentation. Same logic: regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running when oxygen runs low.
items.why: Efficiency seems obviously best. For peak power, throughput beats efficiency every time — which is why sprinters look chemically different from marathoners during a race.

items.title: Bread, beer and yoghurt all use the same biochemical loophole
items.claim: Without oxygen, glycolysis stops because cells run out of NAD+. Yeasts solve this by reducing pyruvate to ethanol (and releasing CO2). Muscles and lactic acid bacteria solve it by reducing pyruvate to lactate. Different products, same problem.

options.text: Both make ATP from the products
Both regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP (2 per glucose); the pyruvate must be 'dealt with' chemically because no oxygen is available to oxidise it via the Krebs cycle

items.reveal_title: NAD+ regeneration as the key step
items.reveal:
Glycolysis converts glucose to 2 pyruvate, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH (reduced electron carrier). For glycolysis to continue running, NAD+ must be regenerated.

Aerobic cells: pyruvate enters mitochondria; Krebs cycle and electron transport oxidise NADH back to NAD+; oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic conditions: no oxygen, so no electron transport. Cells use pyruvate as the electron acceptor instead, dumping electrons from NADH onto it.

Yeasts (alcoholic fermentation): pyruvate -> acetaldehyde (releasing CO2) -> ethanol (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus ethanol and CO2. Bread rises from the CO2; beer accumulates ethanol.

Muscle and lactic acid bacteria (lactic fermentation): pyruvate -> lactate (using NADH, regenerating NAD+). Result: 2 ATP per glucose, plus lactic acid. Soured milk -> yoghurt; cabbage -> sauerkraut.

Aerobic respiration is about 15x more efficient (30-32 ATP vs 2). Fermentation is faster and works without oxygen. Both have their place.

Some organisms (facultative anaerobes like E. coli) switch between the two. Strict aerobes (most animals) die without oxygen within minutes. Strict anaerobes (Clostridium) die WITH oxygen — for them, O2 is toxic.
items.why: Bread, beer, wine, yoghurt and sauerkraut all rely on the same chemical trick to regenerate NAD+. Human civilisation has built food traditions on top of microbial anaerobic biochemistry.

items.title: Cells make energy by pumping ACID uphill
items.claim: Mitochondria spend most of their energy budget pumping protons across the inner membrane against a steep electrochemical gradient. Only after building this acidic outer space do they let the protons flow back through ATP synthase, capturing the energy.
items.prompt: Why not just make ATP directly during electron transport?

options.text: Chemiosmosis lets the cell decouple ENERGY EXTRACTION (electron transport) from ENERGY USE (ATP synthesis); the proton gradient is a rechargeable battery that links any electron donor to any ATP demand
The gradient is a side-effect with no function

items.reveal_title: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis — initially dismissed, then Nobel-winning
items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that ATP synthesis was driven by a proton gradient, not by direct chemistry. Biochemists hated the idea — it seemed to require a 'metabolic battery' instead of a chemical intermediate. Mitchell was right, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to protons. Electrons flowing through the respiratory chain pump protons OUT, building a pH gradient (~ 0.7 units) and an electric potential (~ 150 mV) — together about 200 mV of proton motive force.

ATP synthase is essentially a rotary motor turned by proton flow. The number of protons per ATP is fractional (about 3.7 to 4) because synthase geometry doesn't match the chemistry of ATP cleanly.
items.why: Energy currency feels like chemistry. Living cells use a physical gradient — a battery — as the actual unit of energy transfer.
